Theoretical foundations and mathematical specification

Specification snapshot: 2026-10-21. See the documentation index, metric definitions, and experiment protocol and flowcharts.

1. Task: conditional causal system identification

The project learns an audio processor from synchronized dry/wet recordings. A target device is a dynamical system:

where internal state can represent filter memory, capacitor behavior, gain envelopes, or reverberation. System identification estimates observable input/output behavior; it does not uniquely recover a device's physical circuit.

The trainable approximation is

Here indexes audio blocks; controls are constant within each block. One experiment currently contains one effect family and one sample rate. Device ID and effect type are metadata, not learned embeddings. A multi-device model, reference latent, and arbitrary control set are proposed extensions.

The current neural output is always a dry signal plus a learned residual:

Causality requires for . Zero future input dependence means zero algorithmic lookahead; it does not eliminate audio-interface buffering or callback scheduling latency.

2. Signal-processing foundations

2.1 Sampling, amplitude, and aliasing

A sampled waveform is . Frequencies above fold into the represented band. Even a bandlimited input can produce out-of-band harmonics after a nonlinearity, so causality alone does not prevent aliasing.

At 48 kHz, sample spacing is approximately . All implemented experiments are mono. Loading integer PCM converts its numerical scale into floating-point audio; it does not independently peak-normalize recordings. Verification requires finite audio within full scale, . Model predictions are not clipped or guaranteed to remain in that interval.

Absolute input level is part of nonlinear system behavior. Replacing with generally gives . Independently normalizing dry and wet recordings therefore changes the identification problem and can hide gain errors.

The synthetic distortion is evaluated directly at the configured sample rate, without oversampling or antialias filtering. A proposed antialiased baseline would upsample, apply the nonlinearity, low-pass, and downsample. Such a baseline changes the target definition and must have its own versioned protocol.

2.2 Linear time-invariant systems and FIR convolution

An LTI processor obeys superposition and time-shift invariance. Its causal finite response is

Its frequency response is

The magnitude shapes frequency balance; phase shapes temporal alignment and waveform details. A finite FIR is bounded-input bounded-output stable since . This explains why a cabinet IR is a strong conventional baseline. A neural model needs an additional purpose, such as interpolation, compression, or nonlinear behavior, to justify replacing known convolution.

Drive means coloration amount here, rather than nonlinear gain. For fixed controls these targets remain LTI. Their effective IR is . Either or yields identity, although the evaluator's bypass flag checks only .

At 48 kHz the responses contain 129 and 9600 taps. The reverb is a simple damped cosine fixture, not a diffuse room simulation. Output tail beyond the source length is discarded; explicit appended silence is necessary to evaluate decay after the performance ends.

Let stored latency be samples. Positive latency means the wet path lags dry. The importer performs

where is the common remaining length. Prepared records store original lag and set prepared lag to zero. The importer neither estimates lag nor resamples. Fractional-sample offsets and clock drift require additional preprocessing.

For a sinusoidal target of amplitude , a pure alignment error of samples has approximately

over complete periods. A small time offset can therefore dominate high-frequency waveform loss. Broadband excitation, gain variation, and multiple controls are needed to distinguish candidate processors; agreement on a few notes does not identify a general audio effect.

3. Deep learning foundations and exact architectures

Neural layers compose learned affine maps and nonlinear functions. Supervised learning minimizes empirical error over training pairs; backpropagation applies the chain rule through the layers and differentiable DSP. Generalization is measured on independent source performances. More parameters increase representational capacity, not guaranteed fidelity.

3.1 Causal convolutions, residual learning, and TCN memory

TCNs use dilations to enlarge temporal context without proportionally increasing depth. Residual additions provide a direct feature path through each block. The broader sequence-modeling foundation is Bai, Kolter, and Koltun; this repository uses its own simpler block design.

The input projection is . Each block left-pads by and computes

This indexing matches PyTorch's cross-correlation convention: kernel index 2 acts on the current sample, and index 0 on the oldest sample. It avoids silently reversing a stored FIR kernel. See the Conv1d operator definition.

3.2 Static FiLM conditioning — implemented

FiLM applies feature-wise affine modulation, as introduced by Perez et al.. Here each block has its own linear map:

The convention allows modulation near identity. Parameters are broadcast over time. No condition encoder, learned device embedding, temporal control network, or feature normalization layer exists in this path.

An unconditioned TCN has the same learned response at every drive setting for identical dry input. A conditioned TCN can represent a family of mappings. The small smoke benchmark does not guarantee that conditioning will improve scores under its training budget.

3.3 GRU state and recurrent memory — implemented

Recurrent networks compress preceding input into hidden state. The GRU concept originates in Cho et al.. For the exact operator used here, follow PyTorch's GRU equations, including the placement of the reset gate in the candidate computation.

Let . A one-layer, unidirectional GRU with hidden width computes

The update gate permits persistent memory without an explicit finite receptive-field limit. Useful memory still depends on training and numerical dynamics. Hidden state persists across inference blocks and resets at a new stream. A GRU's existence alone does not establish successful long-tail modeling.

3.4 Differentiable FIR basis — implemented

Known signal structure can be included in an end-to-end trainable system. This is the general motivation of DDSP; the repository's learned FIR basis is a small specific hybrid, rather than a reproduction of the original DDSP model.

Four bias-free basis filters act in parallel:

For stored Conv1d weights, . Basis coefficients are unconstrained linear outputs, without softmax or positivity requirements. At fixed controls the FIR branch is linear, with effective response . It models a residual response, not necessarily the complete wet response.

Smoke spans only ms of samples at 48 kHz; research spans ms. Neither is a long convolutional reverb engine. In particular, a 33-tap FIR cannot exactly express an arbitrary 129-tap cabinet response.

4. Training mathematics and data contract

4.1 Source-disjoint empirical risk

Let be source-performance IDs. Require pairwise empty intersections. Every preset and crop of one performance belongs to the same source split. The verifier rejects shared source IDs and byte-identical dry WAVs across splits. Re-encoded duplicates require additional provenance review.

For a pair sampled from the training set, the optimized loss is

The precise spectral reductions and numerical floors are specified in metrics. The training objective does not include ESR, LSD, adversarial, perceptual-network, latent, or explicit DC losses.

4.2 Context-aware crops

For a crop of scored samples beginning at , the dataset returns preceding dry context of length plus the crop. Samples before the performance start are zero-filled. The model receives samples; loss is computed only on the final outputs.

The history length is

conv1d uses its forced single dilation in this expression. The GRU begins each sampled crop with zero hidden state and warms up only on this context. It does not inherit the true state at the crop boundary. Finite-context convolution has sufficient preceding samples; recurrent long-memory training does not. Stateful truncated backpropagation through time is required before making long-memory claims.

4.3 Backpropagation, clipping, and AdamW

For layer intermediates , backpropagation evaluates products of local Jacobians:

The implementation clips the combined gradient norm to 1 before AdamW. Conceptually , with the operator's numerical safeguard. AdamW then uses first and second moment estimates and decoupled weight decay:

Here ; learning rate is configurable. Unspecified optimizer options use PyTorch defaults, including betas and epsilon . Decoupled weight decay is not an L2 term added to the reported loss. See Loshchilov and Hutter and the AdamW definition.

Training shuffles pairs, uses one random crop per pair per epoch, rejects nonfinite loss, and runs all configured epochs. It saves the epoch with minimum arithmetic mean active validation-pair ESR, without early stopping. Exact bypass examples contribute zero data loss; they are excluded from validation selection. Training-pair weighting, validation-pair averaging, and test source-median aggregation are distinct operations.

CPU execution seeds Python, NumPy, and PyTorch, enables deterministic operations, and sets one PyTorch thread. Dataset/configuration/checkpoint hashes and environment/source identities support reproduction. They do not guarantee identical timing or bitwise results across different software and hardware.

5. Stateful inference and mathematical invariants

The explicit state is . Before a block, concatenate . The TCN/FIR recompute on that concatenation and discard the first outputs. The GRU processes only , beginning with . Update

A new stream uses zero history and hidden state. Bypass still advances state. Callers own state, allowing independent streams without model-global mutable buffers. The initial-state helper creates both tensors even if a branch does not use one.

For fixed controls and equal initial state, the required invariant is

within the numerical tolerance in metrics. This is checked for regular and irregular blocks. Memory used by the explicit float32 state is bytes, excluding parameters, temporary activations, operator workspaces, and host buffers.

Current controls are reapplied to the entire cached TCN audio history when a block is processed. Consequently constant-control streaming parity does not prove equivalence to a sample-wise automated FiLM model. Automation smoothing, time-varying control semantics, and click-free transitions require a separate design and validation. ONNX parity with changing controls verifies agreement with this block API, not an alternative control model.

Finite-context ONNX export uses fixed batch 1 and block size (default 128), with inputs audio , controls , and history ; outputs are audio and next history. GRU models are rejected until explicit recurrent-state export is implemented. Export success is not native callback or plugin acceptance.

6. Proposed extensions and their mathematical contracts

The expressions below formalize research directions. They are not current APIs, implemented losses, or settled production specifications.

6.1 Temporal FiLM and stateful training

Static FiLM uses only user controls. Temporal FiLM instead derives time-varying modulation from summarized features and recurrent state, conceptually

The original Temporal FiLM paper motivates recurrent modulation. A real-time adaptation must specify strictly causal summaries and modulation timing; pooling over a future block cannot modulate earlier samples without lookahead.

For truncated backpropagation, carry hidden state across contiguous chunks, detach its graph at declared boundaries, and reset at performance changes. Choose warmup, truncation length, scored duration, and source ordering before evaluating long-memory effects.

6.2 Long convolution and feedback reverb

Long IR modeling could replace short dense convolution with partitioned FFT convolution. For partition length , an overlap-add/save implementation forms frequency-domain sums such as

with sufficient zero-padding and explicit overlap state. Partition scheduling and any added algorithmic buffering latency must be documented. FFT partitioning is not implemented.

A feedback delay network is another proposed reverb structure:

For this simplified linear network of pure delays, is a sufficient contraction condition. Learned damping filters require their own stability bounds. No FDN exists in the repository; an unconstrained recurrent processor is not automatically a physically meaningful room model.

6.3 Reference-conditioned effect transfer

The desired task estimates effect identity from a reference dry/wet pair, then processes different source content:

Effect modeling estimates a known paired mapping; transfer additionally requires to retain processing behavior while suppressing performance identity. DeepAFx-ST is a relevant reference for inferring effect controls from audio, but does not establish the proposed hybrid's novelty or performance.

One candidate training contract combines reconstruction, same-effect consistency, different-effect separation, and optional control reconstruction:

Positive pairs share effect settings across independent performances; negative pairs differ in settings/effect. A positive consistency term alone admits a constant collapsed embedding. The encoder structure, latent dimension, normalization, negative sampling, margin , and weights remain to be chosen and preregistered. The optional decoder applies only where controls have a defined ground truth.

Reference/source performances must be disjoint from training content, and evaluation must separate unseen content from unseen devices. An encoder can run when loading a reference, while the audio processor remains causal. No encoder, latent training, or cross-content transfer result is currently implemented.

7. Claim boundaries

Current theory supports well-defined, causal, controllable system-identification experiments. Current evidence supports reproducible synthetic engineering checks. It does not establish physical device fidelity, alias suppression, perceptual indistinguishability, hybrid superiority, native real-time safety, or a releasable plugin. Those outcomes require the phase gates and experiment evidence.
